i'll check it out! thanks a ton!

Find things you want to shoot

Shoot a lot

Choose the ones you like and use the guides to figure out what you like about them

Shoot more

It takes a while to get into it and learn what you like/ want to portray, and its (at least for me) a never ending process. There is money in it for some, but there is a lot of competition. I get paid to shoot weddings, and do around 5-15 a week, but its hard work and sometimes difficult to stay passionate about. My best advice is to just shoot a lot, then shoot some more.

deal. i'm gonna get on the ball about it and get after it while i'm energized about it! how do you market yourself? friends? word of mouth? social media? any particular strategies you find that can keep it pretty consistent? also, where could i go to find different styles of photography? anybody you like in particular? thanks for the recommendations!

Honestly I regret showing people my earliest work, since it wasn't very good. If I were to do it over I would just start a anon instagram account or something to put it out there, and a Flickr account to store the large files. Its how I do it now, even after 4+ years taking photos. Its going to take some time. I had about a six month gap before I took a pic that I still think is good. But once that happened, boom, I was even more motivated and able to really understand what I liked about photography.

I think the best way is to just focus on what you like for now, and don't really worry about what random people think, since it could easily set you back. Random likes don't show you how to improve. If you do start sharing, do it sparingly, like once every few days or once a week even. Plus, imagine if you don't share yet and in six months people get really surprised that you not only took up photography, but are already well on your way to being legit.

For the first year I brought my camera everywhere. I shot photos and video everyday, even though I would often delete everything. Study framing and light. http://strobist.blogspot.com/2006/03/lighting-101.html is a good start for lighting and balance, even if you don't have a flash yet. I pretty much just googled any problem or idea I had (I still do.) Buy some magazines and try to break down the frame, settings, and light. Look at the depth, look at the reflection of the light, look at the framing.

I hope this helps, and welcome to the club!

Yeah actually I created my own stipulations that I was only allowed to take one photo each day and it had to be taken with film.
